outcome: Since 26 January 2024 no source I could open reports a prime k·2ⁿ+1 for any of the five odd k below 78557 still listed as open (21181, 22699, 24737, 55459, 67607), so whether 78557 is the least Sierpiński number remains open; the only in-window events are a 2024 partial-covering paper whose results I could not read and a 2026 arXiv disproof of a different conjecture (consecutive Sierpiński numbers) whose AI attribution is inferred from the paper's table scope, not stated for that entry.
problem_asks: (1) Premise: 78557 is a Sierpiński number, i.e. 78557·2ⁿ+1 is composite for every n≥1 (proved by Selfridge in 1962 with the covering set {3,5,7,13,19,37,73}). (2) Minimality, the conjecture itself: 78557 is the least Sierpiński number, i.e. no odd k<78557 has k·2ⁿ+1 composite for all n≥1; equivalently every odd k in [3,78557) has some n with k·2ⁿ+1 prime. Parts (1) and (2) together are what the bullet asks. Conventions: 'Sierpiński number' is taken as an odd k (the standard definition). Erdős #1113 writes n≥0 instead of n≥1; for odd k≥3, k+1 is even and composite, so the two conventions agree on every k in question.

events.what_happened: John Selfridge showed that 78557 is a Sierpiński number, using the covering set {3,5,7,13,19,37,73}: for each residue of n mod 36, one of these primes divides 78557·2ⁿ+1. The result was unpublished at the time. Selfridge conjectured, in private correspondence with Paul Erdős, that 78557 is the least Sierpiński number (Wikipedia, which cites Erdős & Odlyzko 1979 for the correspondence and Guy 2005 for 'now believed').
events.delivers: Establishes only that 78557 is a Sierpiński number (the premise, part 1). It says nothing about whether a smaller Sierpiński number exists.
events.remains: Part 2 entirely: every odd k below 78557 still needs a prime k·2ⁿ+1 (or some other proof that it is not Sierpiński).
events.directly_checkable: The covering can be checked by hand: the multiplicative orders of 2 modulo 3, 5, 7, 13, 19, 37, 73 are 2, 4, 3, 12, 18, 36, 9, so the cover repeats with period 36 in n, and one checks each residue of n mod 36 against the seven primes. I did not re-run this check (a script execution was declined).
events.direction: Supports the premise (78557 is Sierpiński). Silent on the conjecture that 78557 is the least.
events.object: Covering set {3,5,7,13,19,37,73}: every 78557·2ⁿ+1 has a factor in this set, the factor depending on n mod 36. Explicit; not an existence proof.
people: Paul Erdős (private correspondence on the conjecture)

events.what_happened: Nathan Mendelsohn determined that the prime 271129 is a Sierpiński number; it is the second-smallest known (Wikipedia history section).
events.delivers: Shows 271129 is Sierpiński. That is a larger number, so it does not bear on whether a smaller one exists. Discarded for this bullet.
events.direction: Not a minimality result. Consistent with 78557 being the least known.

events.what_happened: Baillie, Cormack and Williams, 'The problem of Sierpiński concerning k·2ⁿ+1', Mathematics of Computation 37 (1981) 229–231 (corrigendum 1982): they narrowed the least odd k₀ with all k·2ⁿ+1 composite to one of 119 numbers between 3061 and 78557 inclusive. Source: a search-result summary of the AMS page; the AMS page returned 403 when I opened it.
events.revisions: Corrigendum published 1982 (AMS listing seen in search results, not opened).
events.delivers: Narrows the candidate set for the least Sierpiński number to 119 odd k in [3061,78557]. Does not, on the summary I have, eliminate any particular k by a prime.
events.remains: Part 2: the least Sierpiński number is confined to the 119-value set, but minimality is not established.

checked_by.what_they_did: Accepted the paper for publication (inferred from publication; referee reports not seen)

events.doubts: Details come from a search summary, not from the paper; the page returned 403.
events.direction: Moves toward the conjecture (narrows candidates) without any counterexample.

events.what_happened: Jaeschke narrowed the candidate set for the least odd k to 91 numbers in the same range (from a search summary; the AMS listing 'On the smallest k such that all k·2ⁿ+1 are composite', Math. Comp. 40 (1983), appeared in search results and was not opened).
events.delivers: Narrows the least-k candidate set to 91 values in [3061,78557] per the summary. No individual elimination identified.

checked_by.what_they_did: Accepted the paper for publication (inferred from publication)

events.doubts: The figure 91 comes from a search summary; the paper was not opened.

events.what_happened: A. S. Izotov (Fibonacci Quarterly 33(3), 1995) showed that certain fourth powers ℓ⁴ are Sierpiński numbers under congruence conditions, without a covering set for all n. Erdős Problems #1113 cites this and the Filaseta–Finch–Kozek 2008 expansion, with m = 734110615000775⁴ as the example.
events.delivers: A Sierpiński number without a covering set (a perfect fourth power). That answers a question about covering systems, not whether 78557 is the least. Discarded for this bullet.
events.object: m = 734110615000775⁴, a Sierpiński number by Izotov's congruence argument (per Erdős #1113). Explicit congruence conditions.

events.what_happened: The Seventeen or Bust distributed project (started March 2002, per search summaries) had 17 candidate k below 78557 at the start. Science News (Ivars Peterson, 7 Jan 2003, opened) reports that five more were then eliminated in rapid succession (k = 46157, 65567, 44131, 69109, 54767), with 'only 12 more to go'. The article lists the initial 17 partly (4847, 5359, 10223, 19249, 21181, ...). The Irvine McLean page gives the prime exponents: 46157 with n=698207, 65567 with n=1013803, 44131 with n=995972, 69109 with n=1157446, 54767 with n=1337287.
events.delivers: Eliminates the five odd k named above (each by a prime k·2ⁿ+1). Leaves 12 candidates at the January 2003 snapshot. It does not settle minimality.
events.remains: Part 2 for the 12 remaining candidates at the snapshot; later eliminations are recorded in other events and sources.

checked_by.who: Seventeen or Bust distributed computing project
checked_by.qualification: Volunteer computing project run by the Seventeen or Bust team; the primes are computer-verified
checked_by.what_they_did: Found the primes; the project reported the eliminations

events.directly_checkable: Each elimination is a single prime k·2ⁿ+1 (exponents above, per the Irvine McLean table). Checking requires a primality certificate; re-running is not feasible here.
events.doubts: The exact dates of the five eliminations are not in the article; 2002 is inferred from 'early last year' in a January 2003 article.
events.direction: Moves toward the conjecture by removing five candidates; no counterexample.
events.object: Primes 46157·2⁶⁹⁸²⁰⁷+1, 65567·2¹⁰¹³⁸⁰³+1, 44131·2⁹⁹⁵⁹⁷²+1, 69109·2¹¹⁵⁷⁴⁴⁶+1, 54767·2¹³³⁷²⁸⁷+1 (exponents from the Irvine McLean table, not from the article). Explicit primes.

events.what_happened: Helm, Moore, Samidoost and Woltman (2008) treated a 'dual' version: the least positive odd k for which both k·2ⁿ+1 and k+2ⁿ are composite. Search summaries say 78557 is the least such k. Their statements disagree on whether this is proved unconditionally or depends on primality of k+2^m for the smaller k. The Integers paper (emis i61) returned 503 and was not opened.
events.delivers: A minimality result for a different problem (the dual problem, with k+2ⁿ also required composite), per the summary. It does not establish minimality for the classical k·2ⁿ+1 problem. Discarded for this bullet.
events.doubts: Search summaries disagree on whether the dual result is unconditional. Not checked against the paper.
events.direction: Different question; no bearing on the classical conjecture.

events.what_happened: PrimeGrid / Seventeen or Bust: the prime 10223·2³¹¹⁷²¹⁶⁵+1 (9,383,761 decimal digits) was found on a volunteer machine (owner Péter Szabolcs, per search summaries of the t5k and UTM pages). The t5k curios page (opened) calls it a 'proven prime'. The Riesel and search summaries give 31 October 2016 as the date. ScienceAlert (opened, dated 27 Nov 2016) says the prime 'eliminates k = 10,223 as a possible Sierpinski number' and leaves five candidates.
events.delivers: Eliminates k = 10223: 10223·2ⁿ+1 is prime for n = 31172165, so 10223 is not Sierpiński. Leaves five open candidates: 21181, 22699, 24737, 55459, 67607.
events.remains: Part 2 for the five remaining values, plus the global conjecture.

checked_by.qualification: Distributed project with an internal double-check of each prime
checked_by.what_they_did: Primality test and a double-check by the project software (per search summaries; the t5k page says only 'proven prime')

events.directly_checkable: A primality certificate for a 9.4-million-digit number; not re-checkable here.
events.direction: Moves toward the conjecture by removing one candidate; no counterexample.
events.object: The prime 10223·2³¹¹⁷²¹⁶⁵+1, explicit (a non-trivial prime, not an existence proof). It shows 10223 is not Sierpiński.
people: Péter Szabolcs (machine owner, per search summaries)

events.what_happened: Chi Zhang, 'A Solution of Sierpinski Problem Based m', arXiv:2106.07376 (math.NT), v1 only, submitted 8 June 2021: a generalisation to base m, giving infinitely many k with k·mⁿ+1 composite for all n under stated congruence conditions. The paper does not mention 78557 (opened).
events.revisions: v1 only (8 June 2021, 8 pages, no venue stated).
events.delivers: Infinitely many base-m Sierpiński-type numbers. A changed question (base m instead of 2). Discarded for this bullet.
events.doubts: Abstract-level read only; the claimed base-m theorem was not checked.

events.what_happened: Filaseta, Groth and Luckner, 'Generalized Sierpiński numbers', Colloquium Mathematicum (2023); arXiv:2305.09219 (from a search result). Shows the existence of odd k with k·aⁿ+1 composite for all a in [2,A] and all n. Not opened; known from search summaries.
events.delivers: A generalisation to many bases at once. A changed question; does not address 78557. Discarded for this bullet.
events.doubts: Known only from a search summary; not opened.

events.what_happened: Jack W. Leventhal, 'Partial coverings and conditions for Sierpiński candidates', Parabola vol. 60 no. 1 (2024). The introduction (search snippet) says it introduces partial covering systems and necessary conditions for a prime counterexample to narrow the candidates and remove them. The PDF's bookmarks (opened through the fetch tool) show sections 'Application to possible Sierpinski numbers' and subsections 'Case 1: k' to 'Case 5: k', and a section on the extended problem. The PDF text did not decode, so the case results were not read. A search summary says the author was a high-school senior; not verified.
events.delivers: As far as I can tell, the stated aim is to narrow and eliminate candidates, and the cases apparently cover five k values. What each case establishes was not readable, so I cannot say whether any case eliminates a k.
events.remains: Part 2, unless one of Cases 1–5 eliminates a k. Every 2024–2026 source I could open still lists the five values as open, which suggests but does not establish that none was eliminated.
events.doubts: Parabola's refereeing practice is not established. The author's background is from a search summary. The results were not read, so no substantive doubt is recorded either way.
events.direction: Unknown from what I read; the stated aim is candidate elimination, not a claim about minimality.

events.what_happened: PrimeGrid's Sierpiński/Riesel base-5 project (sr5) eliminated k = 67612 with a 3.8-million-digit prime on 8 April 2025 (from a search summary; the boinc-af page returned a DNS error and was not opened). The discoverer is named in the summary as Kai Presler.
events.delivers: Eliminates k = 67612 in the base-5 Sierpiński problem. That is a different problem (base 5). Nothing for base 2 or for 78557. Discarded for this bullet.

checked_by.qualification: Distributed project with a primality proof step
checked_by.what_they_did: Found and verified the prime (per search summary)

events.object: A 3.8-million-digit prime of the base-5 Sierpiński form that eliminates k = 67612 (per summary; the exact form and exponent were not read). Explicit.

events.what_happened: Matt Visser, 'Sierpiński's Hypothesis H1', arXiv:2512.22413 (submitted 27 Dec 2025; v2 per the review page). It verifies Sierpiński's 1958 hypothesis H1 (every row of the n×n array of 1..n² contains a prime) for n up to about 10¹⁰, with partial results for larger n. The pith.science page (opened) is an automated AI-referee review (deepseek-v4-flash, 3 Aug 2026) with four major and four minor objections; it says no human expert has reviewed the paper yet.
events.delivers: Verifies a different Sierpiński-named hypothesis (about primes in n×n arrays), not the k·2ⁿ+1 problem. Nothing about 78557. Discarded for this bullet.

checked_by.what_they_did: Generated a T0 review with four major and four minor objections. The main objection is a numeric mismatch: the abstract claims n up to 10,070,368,414 but the body proof reaches 4,553,432,387, and the review flags it. It also asks for the dependence on an external maximal-prime-gap table to be stated.

events.doubts: The automated review flags a range mismatch in the body and a dependence on an external table; the review says it is fallible and that no human has reviewed the paper.

events.what_happened: Tom Adamczewski (listed affiliation Epoch AI), 'OEIS Open: How many conjectures can language models turn into theorems?', arXiv:2608.11941 (v1 posted 12 Aug 2026; v2 13 Aug 2026). In its Appendix A (p. 23 per the OEIS comment) the paper disproves the 2016 OEIS conjecture A270994 (Altug Alkan) that a(n) and a(n)+28 are always consecutive Sierpiński numbers. Witness: n = 162178349052694, where a(n)+4 = 1813934020268071832273 is itself Sierpiński. The covering argument is a system modulo 96 with primes 3, 5, 17, 257, 65537, 97, 673, 193 plus the periodicity of powers of 2. An OEIS comment by Michael De Vlieger (19 Aug 2026) records the disproof and the entry is marked 'Disproved'.
events.revisions: v1 12 Aug 2026; v2 13 Aug 2026 (current). I did not check whether the disproof is in v1.
events.delivers: Disproves the consecutiveness conjecture for A270994 (about the progression 9454129+11184810·n). Gives one Sierpiński number strictly between a(n) and a(n)+28. Says nothing about whether 78557 is the least Sierpiński number.
events.remains: All of part 1 and part 2 of the bullet, untouched.

checked_by.who: Michael De Vlieger (OEIS contributor, as named in the comment)
checked_by.qualification: No mathematical qualification found in my sources
checked_by.what_they_did: Posted an OEIS comment recording the disproof and marked A270994 'Disproved'. No independent check described.

Per the seqfan post (opened), a submission is accepted only if it is a formal Lean proof of the conjecture or of its negation. The A270994 entry links a Spec.lean file under a run directory; I did not open it.

machine_checked.system: Lean (version not stated in what I read)

events.directly_checkable: The witness can be checked by hand from the covering: (a(n)+4)·2ᵐ+1 is divisible by one of the eight listed primes for each m in a residue class mod the period. I did not recompute the arithmetic (a script run was declined).
events.doubts: No doubt about the disproof was found in what I read. Recorded for the later pass: single-author preprint; the Lean file and sorry status were not checked; the model attribution in the next field is inferred.
events.direction: Cuts against the consecutiveness conjecture for A270994. It is irrelevant to whether 78557 is the least Sierpiński number.
events.object: At n = 162178349052694, a(n) = 9454129+11184810n and a(n)+4 = 1813934020268071832273, which the paper says is a Sierpiński number. This gives a Sierpiński number strictly between a(n) and a(n)+28. The covering is explicit (eight primes, modulus 96 system).

disputes.summary: Sources disagree on how many candidates remain. Eight in the Jones (JIS) survey, date not read (10223, 19249, 21181, 22699, 24737, 33661, 55459, 67607). Six in the 2008 Integers summary and the 2014 AMS post (10223 included). Five in Wikipedia, the 2024 Parabola article's PDF bookmarks, the Irvine McLean page (updated 24 Aug 2023), and the t5k glossary (copyright 2026, status undated). The six-to-five drop is 10223 (2016). The eight-to-six drop is consistent with 19249 and 33661, which the Irvine table lists as eliminated.

The minimality conjecture is attributed to Selfridge's private correspondence with Erdős (Wikipedia, citing Erdős & Odlyzko 1979 and Guy 2005). The 1962 covering result is described as unpublished (per the Integers 2008 summary). Not checked against either original.
The 2008 Helm et al. dual result: search summaries disagree on whether it is an unconditional theorem or depends on primality of k+2^m for the smaller k.

summary: I found no reported prime k·2ⁿ+1 for any of the five odd k below 78557 still listed as open (21181, 22699, 24737, 55459, 67607) in any source dated after 26 January 2024, so 78557's minimality is still open and no in-window event settles any part of part 2. The five-value list is what Wikipedia (undated), the t5k Prime Glossary (2026 footer, status undated), the Irvine McLean page (updated 24 Aug 2023) and the 2024 Parabola article's bookmarks all give. The last elimination on the base-2 problem I could confirm is 10223, by the prime 10223·2³¹¹⁷²¹⁶⁵+1 on 31 Oct 2016 (press 27 Nov 2016, opened). The PrimeGrid / Seventeen or Bust status pages returned 503 errors on every attempt, so the 2024–2026 status rests on undated secondary snapshots, and an elimination the snapshots missed cannot be excluded. The one in-window human paper on the problem itself is Leventhal's 2024 Parabola article, which introduces partial coverings aimed at removing candidates and applies them to five cases; its PDF did not decode, so I cannot say what those cases establish. The in-window AI-linked Sierpiński result is Adamczewski's arXiv:2608.11941 (v1 12 Aug 2026), which disproves the 2016 OEIS conjecture A270994 on consecutive Sierpiński numbers by a witness at n = 162178349052694. It is a different question and does not move part 2. Its Appendix A.1 credits 'Claude Fable 5 on OEIS Open Lite' with some resolved conjectures, but no sentence I could read names a model for A270994, and the Spec.lean link is unopened, so the attribution is inferred and recorded as such. Searches for AlphaEvolve, FunSearch, AlphaProof, GPT, Claude and Gemini combined with Sierpiński found nothing on 78557 itself. Two other AI-adjacent items are outside this bullet: a 19 Jun 2026 blog that shares a Gemini-generated report on the prime Sierpiński variant (opened), and a Chinese-language article (search summary only) claiming a GPT-5.6 prime-gap record. Pre-window history is recorded as events: Selfridge's unpublished 1962 covering proof, the 1981 and 1983 narrowing (119 and 91 candidates, from summaries, since the AMS page returned 403), the five 2002 eliminations (Science News, opened), and the 2016 elimination of 10223. Other Sierpiński-named results (the 2008 dual problem, the base-5 elimination of 2025, Visser's 2025 hypothesis H1, Zhang's 2021 base-m paper, Izotov's covering-free fourth powers, Filaseta et al. 2023) are recorded as discarded because they answer different questions.
competing_reading: Read the Leventhal 2024 paper as eliminating some of the five candidates. Its PDF's case structure ('Case 1: k' to 'Case 5: k') could mean one case per remaining k, and if any case closes a k, the in-window status changes and the five-value lists in 2026 sources would be stale. Against this, every 2026 source I opened still lists all five, which points the other way but is itself only an undated snapshot. On the AI side: read the Appendix A.1 sentence as covering A270994, which makes Claude Fable 5 load-bearing on this disproof. Or read it as a table-scope statement that does not say who produced this particular argument, which leaves the AI role unknown. The paper's own text supports only the second reading.
what_would_settle_it: A readable text of the Leventhal Parabola article, with the results of Cases 1–5. Live PrimeGrid Seventeen or Bust statistics showing the remaining k and dated eliminations after 2016. The text of arXiv:2608.11941 Appendix A.1 row for A270994, with the linked Spec.lean (including whether it is sorry-free), and the author's own statement of who found the covering argument. A re-run of the Selfridge covering check and the A270994 witness check, which I could not run here.

judgement.why: The statement asks whether 78557 is the least Sierpiński number. Selfridge's covering settles only the premise that 78557 is Sierpiński, so it is a case, checkable by hand, and pre-snapshot. Each prime that eliminates a candidate k (the five in 2002, 10223 in 2016) settles that k for good. Since the conjecture comes down to finitely many k, I scored these as cases rather than instances, and all of them are pre-snapshot. The 1981 and 1983 narrowings of the candidate set are bounds. Leventhal 2024 has only a year for its date, so after_snapshot is null, and its results were never read, so it has no scope that can be shown. Base-5, hypothesis H1, base-m, multi-base, the dual problem, covering-free powers and the A270994 consecutiveness disproof all answer different questions and are variants. For A270994 the only basis_quote is a table-scope sentence that names no model for this entry, so it cannot support generated. I answered none, and as a variant the event is discarded anyway.
judgement.doubts: The status after 2024 rests on undated secondary snapshots that still list five candidates, because the PrimeGrid pages returned 503. An elimination those snapshots missed cannot be ruled out. Leventhal's Cases 1–5 were never read. The Claude Fable 5 attribution for A270994 is inferred, not stated. Scoring single-k eliminations as case rather than instances was a judgement call, but every such event is pre-snapshot and none tiers as resolved, so the call does not change the outcome.
